text: The assembly will hear an address by his
excellency Godwin Friday, prime minister
and minister for finance, legal affairs
and justice, economic planning and
private sector development of San
Vincent and the Grenadines.
I request the protocol to escort his
excellency and invite his excellency to
address the assembly.
Mr. President,
excellencies,
friends,
greetings from
the government and people of St. Vincent
and the Grenardines.
Mr. President, we congratulate you on
your election to preside over this
session of the General Assembly. You can
count on our support and cooperation.
Secretary General Antonio Gutierrez,
we are extremely grateful to you for
your bold leadership and determined
advocacy for human rights,
justice, and peace.
We thank you for standing up for small
and vulnerable nations.
The theme restoring trust,
managing transformation, a united
nations that delivers for all
speaks directly to the anxieties of our
time
and also to the hopes of small states
like mine.
As we have heard from many speakers in
this chamber,
trust in the multilateral system is
broken.
Hope has retreated
while cynicism and doubt have grown.
Nevertheless,
we hear the insistent calls for justice,
peace, and for a rules-based
international order that applies equally
to all nations.
Mr. President, I come here for the first
time representing my country, St.
Vincent and the Grenadines with a clear
mandate and a commitment that governance
must be transparent,
that individual actions must
consistently
reflect integrity and that public
resources must be used to improve the
lives of ordinary people.
We are a small democratic
multi island Caribbean nation committed
to multilateralism
and the peaceful resolution of disputes.
Those principles serve us well and we
believe should bind all of us in this
chamber.
We in St. Vincent and the Grenadines
experience firsthand
the vulnerability of living on the front
lines of climate change. Having
experienced only two years ago the
sudden destructive power of a category 5
hurricane.
We also feel enormous strains imposed on
small nations and our small open economy
by distant wars that have disrupted
supply chains
and by decisions made in places where
our voice is never heard. Yet we will
not let vulnerability define us or limit
our ambitions.
We will be resilient and will work
individually and collectively to
transcend our vulnerability.
So, Mr. President, we come to this
August assembly
not as mayor petitioners but as partners
to play our part in making our world a
better place.
I come at this point in the debate
having had the privilege of listening to
other leaders who spoke before me. And
Mr. President, I must tell you I was
moved by the hopeful vision, the fiery
passion, the boundless generosity and
caring of many of the speakers.
They lifted my spirit and I am
determined that that is where my spirit
shall remain.
I owe it to the people who sent me here
to be hopeful. I owe it also to people
whom I have never met, who come from
places I have never been to, but who
nevertheless are my brothers and
sisters.
And so that brings us to the task at
hand.
We all know that the United Nations has
its flaws,
but we must not seek to abandon it.
It is what we have made it.
Some, no doubt,
are more culpable than others, but in
one way or another, we are all involved.
We speak of culpability not merely to
point a finger of blame but to
understand better where the solutions
may lie.
We believe profoundly that more than
ever humanity needs the United Nations.
Try to imagine a world without it. Where
would we go to have the conversations we
having now and that we are having
throughout the week?
And that is only the beginning.
As a global institution, the United
Nations is fundamentally
an inclusive space where every nation
can play a role in addressing our common
problems.
A retreat from multilateralism
undermines the interests of small states
and indeed of everyone.
But we acknowledge that our support for
the United Nations must be matched by
our willingness to embrace reform to
make it more effective.
Trust cannot be built or restored by
declarations alone.
It is only when ordinary people see that
cooperation makes their lives safer,
richer, and happier. that trust will be
restored.
Mr. President, let us restore trust
through organizational reform and
greater inclusiveness.
The United Nations governance model
designed in 1945
cannot adequately address the security
and economic challenges of today.
Therefore, we join with other nations in
calling for reform, specifically
of the security council to include a
permanent member from the continent of
Africa with all the attendant rights and
privileges.
Failure to do so will only confirm that
the current composition is not about
governance and fairness, but about
power.
Further, as we proceed with selecting
our next secretary general,
let us be more open and inclusive.
St. Vincent and the Grenadines is
pleased to join other Caribbean
community members in endorsing the
candidacy of her excellency Caroline
Rodriguez Burket of Trinidad of Guyana
and of the region of Latin America and
the Caribbean.
We know her as a distinguished
diplomat, a principled multilateralist,
and a compelling advocate for developing
countries and small states.
Mr. President,
as this is my first time here, like a
tourist, I walked the halls of this
historic building and admired the on the
walls the impressive portraits of the
nine men who have served as Secretary
General since 1946.
And while I appreciated the outstanding
caliber and service of those men, I
nevertheless could not resist thinking
that after eight decades, surely the
time has come for an equally capable
woman to be Secretary General.
We believe
Ambassador Caroline Rodriguez Burkehead
of Guyana is well suited to be that
person.
Mr. President, for small island
developing states, climate change is not
a distant forecast.
It is a present danger and recurring
financial emergency. We suffer the
scourge of sargasm seaweed that damages
our tourism. We worry about the growing
problem of Sahara dust that seriously
degrades our air quality across the
Caribbean.
And of course, we worry constantly about
hurricanes. In July 2024,
Hurricane Barrel struck in Vincent and
the Grenardines and demonstrated once
again how a few hours of extreme weather
can destroy lives,
homes, livelihoods, and infrastructure
built over many years
and set a country back.
Small states cannot continue borrowing
merely to replace what climate related
disasters repeatedly destroy. We cannot
continue to walk up the down escalator
pretending it is development.
Mr. President, we renew our call for the
full operationalization
of the multi-dimensional
vulnerability index so that access to
concessional financing is not
constrained by per capita income but
reflects the real climate risks small
island states face and their limited
capacity to respond to such large
events. We also call for the swift
implementation
of reforms set out in the Antigga and
Barbuda agenda for SIDS.
Further, we support the continuing work
of the Bridgetown initiative to reform
the international financial
architecture,
including automatic debt service
suspension clauses when disaster
strikes. Expanded and rechanneled
special drawing rights and multilateral
development banks that lend like
development partners rather than like
commercial creditors.
Mr. President, we must also accept that
affordable, patient, concessional
capital is not charity to small states.
It is justice for states that contribute
the least to the climate crisis yet bear
the highest costs.
Mr. President, let us restore trust
through the pursuit of peace and
security.
Trust in the international system begins
with the conviction that everyone
matters and that the security of small
states is as precious as that of great
powers.
International conflicts far from our
shores in Ukraine and the Middle East
continue to have devastating
consequences for our daily lives,
disrupting agricultural trade and global
food stability
and driving up fuel prices and shipping
premiums.
We therefore join others here and call
for an immediate end to the war in
Ukraine with full respect for state
sovereignty and territorial integrity
under the UN charter. And likewise, we
call for a permanent ceasefire in the
Middle East, the protection of
civilians, and the realization of a
two-state solution guaranteeing peace
and security for Palestine and Israel.
Mr. President, St. Vincent and the
Grenadines does not stand alone. We
stand with our brothers and sisters in
the Caribbean community, Caraccom,
which is not just a trading block, but a
family whose members in these uncertain
times need each other more than ever.
For us in the Caribbean, peace and
security are paramount concerns in our
diplomatic efforts. Therefore, as we
seek to restore trust, we reaffirm that
Latin America and the Caribbean must
remain a zone of peace where disputes
are settled through peaceful means with
adherence to international law and the
UN charter.
We urge that the territorial dispute
between Venezuela and Guyana be resolved
in this manner
within our hemisphere.
Other unresolved challenges require
immediate principled engagement.
Haiti remains our urgent concern. Nearly
four decades ago, the Trinidadian
Calypsonian David Rudder sang a lament
to Haiti. His words are still relevant
today. I quote, "When there is anguish
in Porto France,
it's still Africa crying.
We are outing fires in far away places.
When our neighbors are burning, I refuse
to believe that we good people will
forever turn our hearts and our eyes
away. Haiti, I am sorry. And the song
goes on.
The insecurity of the Haitian people
plagued by gang violence and political
uncertainty is a pain felt across our
region.
We support the efforts of CARICOM and
this organization to help fund and
provide security to build up critical
institutions and create a viable path to
general elections.
We must confront the reality of arms
trafficking, including assault weapons
that are terrorizing Haitian communities
and indeed communities across the
Caribbean.
We don't make these weapons in the
Caribbean. They are manufactured in
industrial nations and smuggled across
borders into our region into our
countries. We therefore call upon all
countries to take decisive action to
stem the illicit flow of weapons and
ammunitions across borders and into the
Caribbean.
Mr. President, Cuba has long been a
valued member of our Caribbean family.
For more than three decades, this
assembly has said that the economic
embargo imposed in Cuba must end.
Whatever the disagreements exist,
the collective punishment of an entire
population, denying medicine, denying
trade, denying fuel, denying ordinary
development cannot be reconciled with
the charter we all signed. My government
adds its voice to call re a call renewed
year after year in this hall for the
embargo to end.
When earthquake devastating earthquake
struck Venezuela earlier this year,
claiming thousands of lives, St. Vincent
and the Grenadines stood up in
solidarity contributing emergency
assistance through a coordinated
caraccom relief effort.
Mr. President, when tragedy strikes, we
must act as our brothers and sisters
keepers.
This too builds and restores trust among
nations and strengthens
the United Nations.
Mr. President friendship also forms is a
form of trust and I wish in this August
body to recognize our country's 45 years
of diplomatic ties and friendship with
Taiwan that has seen us work together in
development in disaster response,
education and in public health. Taiwan
has shown time and again that they are
prepared to be a responsible member of
the international community.
We renew our call for Taiwan's
meaningful participation in the United
Nations system and its specialized
agencies.
Mr. President, let us also restore trust
through support for reparatory justice.
The past is not the past when its
consequences still shape who is rich and
who is poor in the world today.
The Caribbean community has for over a
decade advanced a 10-point plan for
reparatory justice, seeking
acknowledgement, repair, and genuine
partnership to address the historic
injustices of the enslavement of African
people and the near annihilation of our
indigenous populations.
We are encouraged that in March 2026,
this assembly strongly adopted a
resolution sponsored by Ghana and
supported by the African Union and
CARACOM declaring the trafficking of
enslaved Africans and racialized cattle
enslavement of Africans as the gravest
crime against humanity.
This is a hopeful and historic event and
after the follow-up conference in Accra
in June, momentum grows, so necessary
actions must follow. When the continent
from which our enslaved ancestors were
taken and the islands to which they were
brought in change in chains spoke in one
voice, this chamber listened. The world
listened. We expect that more steps will
follow from discussions that will be
held as part of the Commonwealth heads
of government meeting in Antigga and
Barbuda in November. As I conclude, Mr.
President, we ask how the United Nations
can restore trust while managing
transformation.
In summary, trust is restored when the
smallest and most vulnerable nations
feel they are included and that their
concerns are addressed.
Trust is restored when a national debt
is restructured to be fairer. It is
restored when hurricane response arrives
in time and when the benefits of new
technology such as artificial
intelligence is shared rather than
hoarded and priced out of reach. It is
restored when an embargo denounced in
this chamber is finally lifted, when
peace in a conflict is secured, and when
a historical wrong is made right. Mr.
President, we remain hopeful with
necessary changes in the organization
and in the mindset of those of us who
shape its work. The United Nations will
live up to its name. However, we must
manage this era of transformation
with courage, honesty, and fairness,
and including equally the concerns of
all the peoples of the world who despite
our individual protestations
are inevitably
part of our shared humanity. Thank you
and may God bless us all.
On behalf of the assembly, I wish to
thank the prime minister and minister of
finance, legal affairs and justice,
economic planning and private sector
development of St. Vincent and the
Grenadines.
